cor-block-psd-by-inertia.title: Block Definiteness, a Second Proof
cor-block-psd-by-inertia.html: Let 1≤k≤n−1 and let M=(ABB∗D)∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with A∈Mk(F) and A≻0. Then M≻0⟺M/A≻0,M⪰0⟺M/A⪰0.

cor-capture-bound-revisited.title: The Capture Bound as a Case of Ky Fan
cor-capture-bound-revisited.title_html: The Capture Bound as a Case of Ky Fan
cor-capture-bound-revisited.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp, p=min(m,n), extended by σi=0 for p<i≤m, and let q1,…,qs be an orthonormal list in Fm. Then ∑j=1s‖A∗qj‖2 ≤ ∑i=1sσi2.

cor-courant-fischer-operator.title: Courant–Fischer for a Self-Adjoint Operator
cor-courant-fischer-operator.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F=R or F=C, with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint, with eigenvalues λ1(T)≥⋯≥λn(T) repeated according to multiplicity. Then for every k with 1≤k≤n, λk(T)=mindim⁡U=n−k+1 max0≠v∈U⟨Tv,v⟩⟨v,v⟩=maxdim⁡U=k min0≠v∈U⟨Tv,v⟩⟨v,v⟩, where U runs over the subspaces of V of the stated dimension.

cor-distance-to-singular.title: The Distance to Singularity
cor-distance-to-singular.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be invertible. Then min{‖A−B‖2:B∈Mn(F) singular}=σn(A)=1‖A−1‖2, the minimum being attained at B=An−1. Consequently the relative distance from A to the nearest singular matrix is min{‖A−B‖2:B singular}‖A‖2=σn(A)σ1(A)=1κ2(A), the reciprocal of the spectral condition number of @def-condition-number.

cor-eigenvalue-shift-total.title: Total Eigenvalue Shift
cor-eigenvalue-shift-total.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, v∈Fn, τ∈R, and A~=A+τvv∗. Then ∑i=1n(λi(A~)−λi(A))=τ‖v‖2.

cor-hadamard-from-majorization.title: Hadamard’s Inequality, Second Proof
cor-hadamard-from-majorization.html: Let F=R or F=C, and let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0. Then detA≤a11a22⋯ann, with equality if and only if A is diagonal or some aii=0.

cor-hermitian-eigenvalues-well-condition.title: The Hermitian Eigenvalue Problem Is Perfectly Conditioned in Absolute Terms
cor-hermitian-eigenvalues-well-condition.title_html:
The Hermitian Eigenvalue Problem Is Perfectly Conditioned in Absolute
Terms
cor-hermitian-eigenvalues-well-condition.html: Let A,E∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and write λ(A)=(λ1(A),…,λn(A)) for the decreasing eigenvalue list. Then ‖λ(A+E)−λ(A)‖∞ ≤ ‖E‖2, and the constant 1 is the smallest one for which this holds.

cor-inertia-subspace-characterization.title: What Each Count Is a Maximum Of
cor-inertia-subspace-characterization.title_html: What Each Count Is a Maximum Of
cor-inertia-subspace-characterization.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. n−(A)=max{dim⁡W:⟨Ax,x⟩<0 for every 0≠x∈W};
  2. n+(A)+n0(A)=max{dim⁡W:⟨Ax,x⟩≥0 for every x∈W}, and symmetrically n−(A)+n0(A) is the largest dimension of a subspace on which ⟨Ax,x⟩≤0;
  3. n0(A)=dim⁡nul(A)=n−n+(A)−n−(A).

cor-interlacing-general-submatrix.title: Deleting m Rows and the Same m Columns
cor-interlacing-general-submatrix.title_html: Deleting m Rows and the Same m Columns
cor-interlacing-general-submatrix.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let 0≤m≤n−1, let I⊆{1,…,n} with |I|=n−m, and let B=AI,I. Then λi(A) ≥ λi(B) ≥ λi+m(A)(1≤i≤n−m).

cor-interlacing-inertia.title: A Principal Submatrix Keeps Most of the Inertia
cor-interlacing-inertia.title_html: A Principal Submatrix Keeps Most of the Inertia
cor-interlacing-inertia.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let 0≤m≤n−1, let |I|=n−m and B=AI,I. Write n+(M) and n−(M) for the number of positive and of negative eigenvalues of a Hermitian M, counted with multiplicity. Then n+(B)≤n+(A)≤n+(B)+m,n−(B)≤n−(A)≤n−(B)+m. In particular A⪰0 implies B⪰0, and A≻0 implies B≻0.

cor-ky-fan-diagonal.title: Partial Sums of the Diagonal
cor-ky-fan-diagonal.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with diagonal entries a11,…,ann, and let 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n. Then ∑j=1kaijij ≤ ∑i=1kλi(A), with equality for k=n.

cor-ky-fan-subadditive.title: Subadditivity of the Top Partial Sums
cor-ky-fan-subadditive.title_html: Subadditivity of the Top Partial Sums
cor-ky-fan-subadditive.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let 1≤k≤n. Then ∑i=1kλi(A+B) ≤ ∑i=1kλi(A)+∑i=1kλi(B).

cor-lidskii-special-cases.title: Weyl and Ky Fan as Cases of Lidskii
cor-lidskii-special-cases.title_html: Weyl and Ky Fan as Cases of Lidskii
cor-lidskii-special-cases.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. (One index.) For every i, λn(A−B) ≤ λi(A)−λi(B) ≤ λ1(A−B), and in particular |λi(A)−λi(B)|≤‖A−B‖2.
  2. (An initial segment.) For every k, ∑i=1kλi(A)−∑i=1kλi(B) ≤ ∑i=1kλi(A−B).

cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone.title: The Loewner Order Compares Every Eigenvalue
cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone.title_html: The Loewner Order Compares Every Eigenvalue
cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with A⪰B. Then λi(A) ≥ λi(B)for every i=1,…,n.

cor-orthogonal-polynomial-zeros-interlac.title: Zeros of Orthogonal Polynomials Interlace
cor-orthogonal-polynomial-zeros-interlac.html:
Let (pk) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence of an inner product on R[x] to which @thm-three-term-recurrence applies, with coefficients ak and bk>0; for the node inner product on R[x]≤n read everything below for k+1≤n. For k≥1 let Tk (the Jacobi matrix of the sequence) be the k×k real symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal a0,a1,…,ak−1 and entries b1,…,bk−1 just above and just below it.

  1. pTk=pk; so the roots of pk are the eigenvalues of Tk, and they are real and distinct.
  2. If r1>⋯>rk+1 are the roots of pk+1 and s1>⋯>sk those of pk, then r1>s1>r2>s2>⋯>sk>rk+1.

cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone.title: Shifted Reciprocals
cor-shifted-inverse-operator-monotone.html: For every s≥0, the function t↦−1/(t+s) is operator monotone on (0,∞). For every s>0, so is t⟼tt+s=1−st+s.

cor-singular-value-perturbation.title: Singular Values Are Perfectly Conditioned
cor-singular-value-perturbation.html: Let A,E∈Mm×n(F). Then |σi(A+E)−σi(A)|≤‖E‖2for every 1≤i≤n. No hypothesis is placed on A or on E.

cor-trace-min.title: The Bottom Partial Sums as a Minimum
cor-trace-min.title_html: The Bottom Partial Sums as a Minimum
cor-trace-min.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let 1≤k≤n. Then ∑i=n−k+1nλi(A)=min{tr(Q∗AQ):Q∗Q=Ik}, the minimum being attained at the bottom k eigenvectors.

cor-weyl-monotone.title: Perturbation, Two-Sided
cor-weyl-monotone.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then for every i, λi(A)+λn(B) ≤ λi(A+B) ≤ λi(A)+λ1(B).

cor-weyl-perturbation.title: Hermitian Eigenvalues Are 1-Lipschitz
cor-weyl-perturbation.html: Let A,E∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then |λi(A+E)−λi(A)| ≤ ‖E‖2for every i=1,…,n.

cor-weyl-rank-bound.title: A Rank-r Perturbation Shifts the Index by r
cor-weyl-rank-bound.title_html: A Rank-r Perturbation Shifts the Index by r
cor-weyl-rank-bound.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let r≥0 be an integer, and suppose rankB≤r. Then λi+r(A+B) ≤ λi(A)(1≤i, i+r≤n),λi(A) ≤ λi−r(A+B)(i≤n, i−r≥1).

def-compression.title: Compression to a subspace
def-compression.html: Let A∈Mn(F), let 1≤k≤n, and let q1,…,qk be an orthonormal list in Fn, so that the matrix Q∈Mn×k(F) with these columns satisfies Q∗Q=Ik. The compression of A to W=span(q1,…,qk) with respect to this basis is the k×k matrix Q∗AQ,(Q∗AQ)ij=⟨Aqj,qi⟩.

def-flag-adapted-list.title: Flags of a given type, and adapted lists
def-flag-adapted-list.title_html: Flags of a given type, and adapted lists
def-flag-adapted-list.html: Let F=R or C, and let 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n be an index set. A flag of type (i1,…,ik) in Fn is a list W=(W1,…,Wk) of subspaces of Fn with W1⊆W2⊆⋯⊆Wkanddim⁡Wj=ij  for every j. A list (x1,…,xk) of vectors of Fn is adapted to W if it is orthonormal and xj∈Wj for every j.

def-inertia-triple.title: The Inertia Triple
def-inertia-triple.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, with eigenvalues λ1(A)≥⋯≥λn(A) listed with multiplicity. Write n+(A), n−(A) and n0(A) for the numbers of indices i with λi(A)>0, with λi(A)<0 and with λi(A)=0, and set In(A):=(n+(A), n−(A), n0(A))∈N3. Triples are added entrywise.

def-majorization.title: Majorization
def-majorization.html:
Let n≥1 and let x,y∈Rn be real vectors with the same number of entries. We say that x is majorized by y, and write x≺y, if

  1. ∑i=1kxi↓≤∑i=1kyi↓ for every k=1,…,n−1; and
  2. ∑i=1nxi=∑i=1nyi (equal totals).

We say that x is weakly majorized by y, and write x≺wy, if the inequality in (M1) holds for every k=1,…,n, including k=n, and (M2) is dropped.

def-operator-monotone.title: Operator Monotone and Operator Convex Functions
def-operator-monotone.title_html: Operator Monotone and Operator Convex Functions
def-operator-monotone.html:
Let I⊆R be an interval and let f:I→R.

  1. f is operator monotone on I if, for every size n≥1 and every pair of Hermitian matrices A,B∈Mn(F) whose spectra lie in I, A⪰B⟹f(A)⪰f(B).
  2. f is operator convex on I if, for every size n≥1, every pair of Hermitian matrices A,B∈Mn(F) whose spectra lie in I, and every θ∈[0,1], f(θA+(1−θ)B)⪯θf(A)+(1−θ)f(B). It is operator concave on I if −f is operator convex on I.

Here f(A) is the matrix of @def-function-of-normal-operator.

def-rayleigh-quotient.title: Rayleigh Quotient
def-rayleigh-quotient.html:
Let F be R or C and let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. The Rayleigh quotient of A is the function RA(x):=⟨Ax,x⟩⟨x,x⟩, defined at every x∈Fn with x≠0, and at no other vector.

For a self-adjoint operator T on a finite-dimensional inner product space V over F, the same formula RT(v)=⟨Tv,v⟩/⟨v,v⟩, for v≠0, defines the Rayleigh quotient of T.

def-secular-function.title: Secular function
def-secular-function.html: Let A=diag(d1,…,dn) with d1,…,dn∈R, let v∈Fn and let τ∈R. The secular function of the update A+τvv∗ is f(λ):=1+τ∑i=1n|vi|2di−λ, defined for every real λ other than d1,…,dn. The equation f(λ)=0 is the secular equation.

exm-loewner-eigenvalue-check.title_html: Checking the corollary on a pair
exm-loewner-eigenvalue-check.html: Let A=(4113) and B=(2112). Then A−B=diag(2,1), which is positive semidefinite, so A⪰B. The eigenvalues of B are 3 and 1, from trace 4 and determinant 3; those of A are 7±52≈4.618, 2.382, from trace 7 and determinant 11. So λ1(A)≈4.618≥3=λ1(B) and λ2(A)≈2.382≥1=λ2(B), as the corollary demands. Note that the two gaps, 1+52≈1.618 and 5−52≈1.382, are different: the corollary orders the eigenvalues, and says nothing about moving them by the same amount.

exm-rayleigh-identity-and-projection.title: Two matrices whose quotient is forced
exm-rayleigh-identity-and-projection.title_html: Two matrices whose quotient is forced
exm-rayleigh-identity-and-projection.html:
Two further cases, at opposite extremes.

  1. The identity. RI(x)=⟨x,x⟩/⟨x,x⟩=1 for every x≠0. The quotient is constant, and the constant is the only eigenvalue. More generally RcI≡c for real c.
  2. An orthogonal projection. Let P∈Mn(F) be the matrix of the orthogonal projection onto a subspace U, so P2=P and P∗=P (@thm-idempotent-orthogonal-iff-selfadjoint). Then ⟨Px,x⟩=⟨P2x,x⟩=⟨Px,Px⟩=‖Px‖2, so RP(x)=‖Px‖2‖x‖2∈[0,1], the fraction of x that survives the projection. Since ‖x‖2=‖Px‖2+‖x−Px‖2 by @thm-pythagoras, it equals 1 exactly when Px=x, that is on U∖{0}, and 0 exactly when Px=0, that is on U⊥∖{0} — matching the eigenvalues 1 and 0 of P.

exm-rayleigh-non-example.title: Change one word: drop Hermitian
exm-rayleigh-non-example.html:
Take A=(0100)∈M2(C), which is not Hermitian, and form ⟨Ax,x⟩/⟨x,x⟩ anyway. At x=(1,i) the numerator is ⟨(i,0),(1,i)⟩=i⋅1―=i and the denominator is 2, so the quotient is i/2, which is not real. The clause that fails is the word Hermitian in @def-rayleigh-quotient, and it fails at the first step: @prp-self-adjoint-immediate (a) is what made the numerator real, and its hypothesis is gone.

Over R the failure is quieter and worse. For A=(0−110)∈M2(R) and real x=(x1,x2), ⟨Ax,x⟩=−x2x1+x1x2=0, so the quotient is real, and identically 0. It is perfectly well behaved and tells us nothing: A has no real eigenvalue at all, and there is no interval [λn,λ1] for the quotient to describe.

exm-wielandt-selection.html: Let A=diag(4,2,1,−1)∈M4(R), take the index set (2,4), and take the flag W1=span((1,1,0,0), e4) ⊂ W2=R4, of type (2,4). Show that the naive attempt, choosing xj∈Wj∩Lij for each j separately, cannot produce an adapted list. Then follow the proof of part (a) to produce one with sum at most λ2(A)+λ4(A).

exr-cauchy-interlacing-a1.title: A1
exr-cauchy-interlacing-a1.html:
1. State @thm-cauchy-interlacing, and say which hypothesis on A and which hypothesis on the submatrix are used.
  2. Let A∈M6(C) be Hermitian and let B=AI,I with |I|=4. Which eigenvalues of A bound λ3(B) above and below?
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if b≠0 then the interlacing between (Bbb∗c) and B is strict.
  4. Explain why a principal submatrix of a positive semidefinite matrix is positive semidefinite, in one sentence, without using interlacing.
  5. Give a 2×2 matrix with real eigenvalues whose (1,1) entry is larger than both of them.

exr-cauchy-interlacing-b1.title: B1: Interlacing in integers
exr-cauchy-interlacing-b1.html: Let A=(012102223). Compute the eigenvalues of A and of all three of its 2×2 principal submatrices, and exhibit the interlacing in each case. Hence say, for each corner, whether the interlacing is strict.

exr-cauchy-interlacing-b2.title: B2: Bounds without a characteristic polynomial
exr-cauchy-interlacing-b2.title_html: B2: Bounds without a characteristic polynomial
exr-cauchy-interlacing-b2.html:
Let A∈M4(R) be symmetric with A=(7∗∗∗∗2∗∗∗∗−3∗∗∗∗1), the entries marked ∗ being unknown.

  1. What do @cor-interlacing-general-submatrix and @exm-diagonal-entries-interlace say about λ1(A) and λ4(A)?
  2. Suppose in addition that A{1,2},{1,2}=(7442). Improve the lower bound on λ1(A), and give a lower bound on λ2(A).

exr-cauchy-interlacing-b3.title: B3: Deciding strictness
exr-cauchy-interlacing-b3.html:
For each of the following bordered matrices A=(Bbb⊤c), decide without computing pA whether the interlacing between A and B is strict, and justify with @thm-bordered-matrix.

  1. B=diag(3,1), b=(0,1), c=0.
  2. B=diag(3,1), b=(2,−1), c=5.
  3. B=(4004), b=(1,2), c=0.

exr-cauchy-interlacing-c1.title: C1: Rank under compression
exr-cauchy-interlacing-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian of rank r, and let B=AI,I with |I|=n−m.

  1. Prove that rankB≥r−2m.
  2. Show that the bound is attained, by exhibiting for each n and each m≤n/2 a Hermitian A of rank 2m with a principal submatrix of size n−m and rank 0.

exr-cauchy-interlacing-c2.title: C2: The converse, in the smallest case
exr-cauchy-interlacing-c2.title_html: C2: The converse, in the smallest case
exr-cauchy-interlacing-c2.html:
@thm-cauchy-interlacing says that the spectrum of a corner interlaces the spectrum of the whole. This exercise asks whether every interlacing pattern occurs.

  1. Let λ1>μ1>λ2 be real numbers. Find b∈R and c∈R such that A=(μ1bbc) has eigenvalues λ1 and λ2.
  2. Deduce that for n=2 the interlacing condition of @thm-cauchy-interlacing is not merely necessary but also sufficient.
  3. Explain why the strict hypothesis λ1>μ1>λ2 may be relaxed to λ1≥μ1≥λ2.

Hint: match the trace and the determinant.

exr-cauchy-interlacing-c3.title: C3: How far apart can the extremes be
exr-cauchy-interlacing-c3.title_html: C3: How far apart can the extremes be
exr-cauchy-interlacing-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. Prove that λ1(A)−λn(A)≥maxi,j |aii−ajj|.
  2. Prove that λ1(A)−λn(A)≥2maxi≠j|aij|.

Hint for (b): look at a 2×2 principal submatrix.

exr-courant-fischer-a1.title: A1
exr-courant-fischer-a1.html:
1. State both lines of @thm-courant-fischer, being careful about which dimension goes with which line.
  2. State @lem-subspace-intersection, and say at which point of the proof of @thm-courant-fischer it is used and what it is used on.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: λk(A)=mindim⁡W=kmax0≠x∈WRA(x).
  4. Write the first line of @thm-courant-fischer in the increasing-index convention μ1≤⋯≤μn.
  5. Explain in one or two sentences why @thm-loewner-basic (b) could not be extended to intermediate eigenvalues by the argument Chapter 12 used, and what @thm-courant-fischer supplies instead.

exr-courant-fischer-b1.title: B1: Both forms on a diagonal matrix
exr-courant-fischer-b1.title_html: B1: Both forms on a diagonal matrix
exr-courant-fischer-b1.html:
Let A=diag(5,2,−1)∈M3(R) and k=2.

  1. Give the witness subspace for the max–min form, compute the minimum of RA on it, and check the value against @thm-courant-fischer.
  2. Do the same for the min–max form.
  3. Put u=12(0,1,1). Compute the minimum of RA over the non-zero vectors of span(e1,u), and over those of span(e2,e3), and verify that neither subspace beats the witness in (a).

exr-courant-fischer-b2.title: B2: Shifting by a multiple of the identity
exr-courant-fischer-b2.title_html: B2: Shifting by a multiple of the identity
exr-courant-fischer-b2.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let c∈R. Prove that λk(A+cI)=λk(A)+c for every k, using the first line of @thm-courant-fischer for both matrices.

exr-courant-fischer-b3.title: B3: Comparing two matrices
exr-courant-fischer-b3.html: Let A=(3113),B=(2001). Verify that A⪰B, compute both eigenvalue lists, and check @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone. Check whether λ1(A)−λ1(B)≤λ1(A−B) holds for this pair. (Whether it holds for every pair is a question for Section 3.)

exr-courant-fischer-c1.title: C1: The definite generalized eigenvalue problem
exr-courant-fischer-c1.title_html: C1: The definite generalized eigenvalue problem
exr-courant-fischer-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with A≻0, and recall @def-generalized-eigenvalue: λ is a generalized eigenvalue of the pair (A,B) when Bx=λAx for some x≠0. Define the generalized Rayleigh quotient RA,B(x)=⟨Bx,x⟩⟨Ax,x⟩(x≠0).

  1. Prove that RA,B is well defined and real-valued.
  2. Put C=A−1/2BA−1/2. Prove that C is Hermitian and that det(B−λA)=det(A)det(C−λI), so that the generalized eigenvalues of (A,B), with multiplicity, are exactly the eigenvalues of C. Write them d1≥⋯≥dn.
  3. Prove that for every k, dk=mindim⁡W=n−k+1 max0≠x∈WRA,B(x).

Hint for (c): the substitution x=A−1/2y.

exr-courant-fischer-c2.title: C2: How much weaker the eigenvalue comparison is
exr-courant-fischer-c2.title_html: C2: How much weaker the eigenvalue comparison is
exr-courant-fischer-c2.html:
1. Give Hermitian A,B∈M2(R) with λi(A)≥λi(B) for i=1,2 but A⪰̸B. So the converse of @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone is false.
  2. Prove that if A and B are Hermitian with λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i and trA=trB, then λi(A)=λi(B) for every i.
  3. Prove that if A⪰B and trA=trB, then A=B.

exr-courant-fischer-c3.title: C3: Does enlarging the field change the answer?
exr-courant-fischer-c3.title_html: C3: Does enlarging the field change the answer?
exr-courant-fischer-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric. It may be read as an element of Mn(C), where it is Hermitian, and then @thm-courant-fischer minimizes over a much larger collection of subspaces.

  1. Prove that the eigenvalue lists of A over R and over C, with multiplicity, are the same.
  2. Deduce that for every k, minW⊆Rndim⁡W=n−k+1max0≠x∈WRA(x)=minW⊆Cndim⁡W=n−k+1max0≠x∈WRA(x).
  3. Show that the second minimum really does range over strictly more subspaces, by exhibiting a one-dimensional subspace of C2 that contains no non-zero real vector.

exr-inertia-revisited-a1.title: A1
exr-inertia-revisited-a1.html:
1. Define In(A) for a Hermitian A, and say what n++n− equals.
  2. State the subspace description of n+(A) and name the subspace that attains it.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify: “n0(A) is the largest dimension of a subspace on which ⟨Ax,x⟩ vanishes identically.”
  4. State @thm-haynsworth, with all hypotheses.
  5. A congruence preserves the inertia of a Hermitian matrix. Does it preserve the eigenvalues, the trace, or the rank? Justify each answer.

exr-inertia-revisited-b1.title: B1: Two inertias by Schur complement
exr-inertia-revisited-b1.title_html: B1: Two inertias by Schur complement
exr-inertia-revisited-b1.html:
Find the inertia of each of the following, using @thm-haynsworth with the leading 2×2 block, and compute no eigenvalues.

  1. M=(21111010−1).
  2. N=(10110−11011201001).

exr-inertia-revisited-b2.title: B2: How much can a rank-two perturbation do?
exr-inertia-revisited-b2.title_html: B2: How much can a rank-two perturbation do?
exr-inertia-revisited-b2.html:
Let A∈M6(R) be symmetric with In(A)=(4,1,1), and let E be symmetric with rankE=2.

  1. Which values of n+(A+E) does @thm-inertia-rank-perturbation allow?
  2. Show that the two extreme values are both achieved, for suitable A and E.
  3. Can A+E be negative definite? Justify.

exr-inertia-revisited-b3.title: B3: A bordered matrix
exr-inertia-revisited-b3.html:
Let D∈Mn(R) be symmetric and invertible, let b∈Rn and c∈R, and put M=(Dbb⊤c).

  1. Express In(M) in terms of In(D) and the scalar s=c−b⊤D−1b.
  2. Take D=diag(1,−1) and b=(1,1). Compute In(M) for c=0, c=1 and c=−1.
  3. For which c is M singular?

exr-inertia-revisited-c1.title: C1: How large can a subspace be on which the form vanishes?
exr-inertia-revisited-c1.title_html: C1: How large can a subspace be on which the form vanishes?
exr-inertia-revisited-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with In(A)=(n+,n−,n0). Call a subspace W≤Fn totally isotropic for A if ⟨Ax,x⟩=0 for every x∈W; for real symmetric A this is the notion of Chapter 13 §07, in the form that section derives from polarization.

  1. Prove that every totally isotropic W satisfies dim⁡W≤n0+min(n+,n−).
  2. Construct a totally isotropic subspace of dimension exactly n0+min(n+,n−).
  3. Deduce that the largest dimension of a totally isotropic subspace equals n0 if and only if A is positive semidefinite or negative semidefinite.

Hint: for (a), a totally isotropic subspace satisfies both inequalities of @cor-inertia-subspace-characterization (b). For (b), pair up a positive eigenvector with a negative one.

exr-inertia-revisited-c2.title: C2: The inertia of a Hermitian dilation
exr-inertia-revisited-c2.title_html: C2: The inertia of a Hermitian dilation
exr-inertia-revisited-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank r, and let H(A)=(0AA∗0)∈Mm+n(F) be the Hermitian dilation of @prp-hermitian-dilation.

  1. Prove that In(H(A))=(r, r, m+n−2r).
  2. Deduce a formula for rankA in terms of the inertia of H(A), and check that it gives rank0=0.
  3. Verify (a) for A=(102011).

exr-inertia-revisited-c3.title: C3: Inertia from the leading principal minors
exr-inertia-revisited-c3.title_html: C3: Inertia from the leading principal minors
exr-inertia-revisited-c3.html:
Let M∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and suppose that every leading principal submatrix Mk∈Mk(F) (rows and columns 1,…,k) is invertible, for k=1,…,n. Write dk=detMk and d0=1.

  1. Prove that for 2≤k≤n the Schur complement Mk/Mk−1 is the scalar dk/dk−1.
  2. Deduce that In(M)=(n+,n−,0), where n− is the number of indices k∈{1,…,n} with dk/dk−1<0 — that is, the number of sign changes in the sequence d0,d1,…,dn.
  3. Apply this to the matrix M of @exm-haynsworth-3x3 and compare.

Hint: for (b), induct on k using @thm-haynsworth.

exr-majorization-and-schur-a1.title: A1
exr-majorization-and-schur-a1.html:
1. State the definitions of x≺y and x≺wy for x,y∈Rn.
  2. Decide whether (2,1,1)≺(2,2,0), and whether (2,2,0)≺(2,1,1).
  3. True or false: if x≺y, then x1≤y1. Justify your answer.
  4. State @thm-schur-majorization. Which result of §06 is it a restatement of?
  5. State @thm-schur-horn. Which half is proved by induction on n, and which lemma does each step of that induction use?

exr-majorization-and-schur-b1.title: B1: Determine which pairs are comparable
exr-majorization-and-schur-b1.title_html: B1: Determine which pairs are comparable
exr-majorization-and-schur-b1.html:
For each pair, determine whether x≺y and whether x≺wy. Where a relation fails, name the exact clause and the value of k at which it fails. Justify your answer.

  1. x=(2,2,1,1), y=(3,2,1,0).
  2. x=(0,3,1), y=(4,0,0).
  3. x=(1,1,0), y=(2,1,0).
  4. x=(−1,2,2), y=(3,0,0).
  5. x=(3,1,1,1), y=(2,2,2,0); decide also whether y≺x.

exr-majorization-and-schur-b2.title: B2: Schur’s theorem for one matrix
exr-majorization-and-schur-b2.title_html: B2: Schur’s theorem for one matrix
exr-majorization-and-schur-b2.html:
Let A=(322240207).

  1. Verify that (2,1,4), (−1,−2,1) and (−3,2,1) are eigenvectors of A, and find 𝛌λ(A).
  2. Write down d(A) and verify every clause of 𝛌d(A)≺λ(A).
  3. Hence verify Hadamard’s inequality (@thm-hadamard-inequality) for A.

exr-majorization-and-schur-b3.title: B3: Which diagonals are ruled out?
exr-majorization-and-schur-b3.title_html: B3: Which diagonals are ruled out?
exr-majorization-and-schur-b3.html:
A Hermitian 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues 5,1,0. For each proposed list of diagonal entries, determine whether @thm-schur-majorization rules it out. Justify your answer.

  1. 4,2,0.
  2. 6,0,0.
  3. 3,3,1.
  4. 2,2,2.
  5. −1,4,3.

For the lists that are not ruled out, what does @thm-schur-horn add?

exr-majorization-and-schur-c1.title: C1: Majorization squeezes the range
exr-majorization-and-schur-c1.html:
1. Prove that if x≺y, then yn↓≤xn↓≤x1↓≤y1↓.
  2. Deduce that every diagonal entry of a Hermitian A lies in [λn(A),λ1(A)].
  3. Show that the conclusion of (b), together with equal totals, does not imply majorization. Prove that no Hermitian matrix has eigenvalues 4,1,1,0 and diagonal entries 3,3,0,0, although every one of these entries lies in [0,4] and the totals agree.

exr-majorization-and-schur-c2.title: C2: A weaker determinant bound
exr-majorization-and-schur-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) with A⪰0.

  1. Prove that detA≤(1ntrA)n, with equality if and only if A=cI for some real c≥0.
  2. Prove that a11⋯ann≤(1ntrA)n. Deduce that Hadamard’s inequality (@thm-hadamard-inequality) always implies the bound in (a).
  3. For A=(202052226), whose eigenvectors are (1,2,3), (1,−2,1) and (−4,−1,2), compute the three numbers detA, a11a22a33 and (13trA)3.

exr-majorization-and-schur-c3.title: C3: The possible diagonals form a convex set
exr-majorization-and-schur-c3.title_html: C3: The possible diagonals form a convex set
exr-majorization-and-schur-c3.html:
For x∈Rn and 1≤k≤n, write sk(x)=x1↓+⋯+xk↓.

  1. Prove that sk(x)=max{∑i∈Ixi:I⊆{1,…,n}, |I|=k}.
  2. Deduce that sk(x+y)≤sk(x)+sk(y) for all x,y∈Rn.
  3. Let 𝛌λ∈Rn. Prove that if 𝛌d≺λ and 𝛌d′≺λ, then 𝛌td+(1−t)d′≺λ for every 0≤t≤1.
  4. Hence show that if A and B are Hermitian n×n matrices with the same eigenvalues, then for every 0≤t≤1 there is a real symmetric matrix with those eigenvalues and diagonal td(A)+(1−t)d(B).

Hint for (a): if v1≥⋯≥vk are the entries xi, i∈I, in decreasing order, count how many entries of x are at least vj.

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-a1.title: A1
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-a1.html:
1. Define “f is operator monotone on I”, and say what the clause “for every n” ranges over.
  2. Explain why an operator monotone function is increasing, and name an increasing function that is not operator monotone.
  3. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f:I→R is increasing and A⪰B are Hermitian with spectra in I, then λi(f(A))≥λi(f(B)) for every i.
  4. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if A,B are Hermitian of the same size and λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i, then A⪰B.
  5. Which of t↦t2 and t↦−1/t is operator monotone on (0,∞), and which is operator convex there?
  6. What does this section prove about Loewner’s theorem?

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b1.title: B1: Which are operator monotone?
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b1.html:
Determine which of the following functions are operator monotone on the interval given. Justify your answer.

  1. f(t)=5+4t on R.
  2. f(t)=3−2t on R.
  3. f(t)=2−3t+1 on (0,∞).
  4. f(t)=tt+2 on (0,∞).
  5. f(t)=t2 on [0,∞).

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b2.title: B2: One pair, three functions
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b2.html:
Let A=(3111),B=(2111).

  1. Show that A⪰B≻0.
  2. Compute A−1 and B−1, and verify directly that B−1⪰A−1, as @prp-inverse-operator-monotone predicts.
  3. Show that A2⪰̸B2 by exhibiting a vector x with x⊤(A2−B2)x<0.
  4. Compute the eigenvalues of A2 and B2, and verify that λi(A2)≥λi(B2) for i=1,2. Hence explain which result of this section (c) and (d) illustrate together.

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b3.title: B3: The convexity identity in numbers
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b3.title_html: B3: The convexity identity in numbers
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-b3.html: With A and B as in B2 and θ=12, compute M=12A2+12B2−(12A+12B)2 directly, confirm that M=14(A−B)2, and hence conclude that (12(A+B))2⪯12(A2+B2).

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c1.title: C1: Iterated square roots
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c1.html:
1. Let A⪰B⪰0. Prove that A1/4⪰B1/4, where A1/4 is f(A) for f(t)=t1/4 on [0,∞).
  2. Deduce that t↦t1/2k is operator monotone on [0,∞) for every integer k≥0.
  3. Explain why the argument of (b) cannot reach t↦t3/4, and say where the operator monotonicity of tp for every p∈(0,1) is proved.

Hint for (a): the positive square root is unique.

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c2.title: C2: The reciprocal is operator convex
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c2.title_html: C2: The reciprocal is operator convex
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c2.html:
1. Let G∈Mn(F) with G≻0. Prove that the 2n×2n matrix (GInInG−1) is Hermitian and ⪰0.
  2. Let A,B≻0 be of the same size and θ∈[0,1]. Prove that (θA+(1−θ)B)−1 ⪯ θA−1+(1−θ)B−1, that is, t↦1/t is operator convex on (0,∞).
  3. Deduce that t↦−1/t is both operator monotone and operator concave on (0,∞).

Hint: Schur complements.

exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c3.title: C3: The cube needs its own witness
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c3.title_html: C3: The cube needs its own witness
exr-monotone-matrix-functions-c3.html:
1. With A and B as in B2, show that A3⪰̸B3. Conclude that t↦t3 is not operator monotone on [0,∞).
  2. One might hope to deduce (a) from the failure of t↦t2. Suppose t↦t3 were operator monotone on [0,∞). Applying it and t↦t1/2 (@prp-square-root-monotone) to both sides of A⪰B⪰0, repeatedly and in any order, yields inequalities Aq⪰Bq for certain exponents q. Show that every such q has the form 3j/2k with integers j,k≥0, and that 2 never has this form. Explain why this means (a) needed a witness of its own.

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-a1.title: A1
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-a1.html:
1. Define the compression of A to a subspace, and say what has to be checked before the phrase “the eigenvalues of the compression” makes sense.
  2. State @thm-ky-fan, including where the maximum is attained.
  3. Explain why the maximum in @thm-ky-fan does not need an appeal to compactness.
  4. Is A↦λ1(A) convex on the Hermitian matrices? Is A↦λn(A)? Justify each answer.
  5. State @thm-poincare-separation and say which case of it is @thm-cauchy-interlacing.

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b1.title: B1: A compression, and two bounds
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b1.title_html: B1: A compression, and two bounds
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b1.html:
Let A=diag(5,0,−2) and let q1=13(1,2,2), q2=13(2,1,−2).

  1. Verify that (q1,q2) is orthonormal and compute the compression B of A to span(q1,q2).
  2. Find the eigenvalues of B and verify @thm-poincare-separation.
  3. Compare trB with the bound of @thm-ky-fan, and say how far this subspace is from optimal.

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b2.title: B2: Reading the sums off the spectrum
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b2.title_html: B2: Reading the sums off the spectrum
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b2.html:
A Hermitian A∈M4(R) has eigenvalues 6,4,1,−3.

  1. Compute max{tr(Q⊤AQ):Q⊤Q=Ik} for k=1,2,3,4.
  2. Compute the corresponding minima, using @cor-trace-min.
  3. For A=diag(6,4,1,−3) and q1=12(1,1,0,0), q2=12(0,0,1,1), compute tr(Q⊤AQ) and check it against (a) and (b).

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b3.title: B3: Subadditivity, and how loose it can be
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b3.title_html: B3: Subadditivity, and how loose it can be
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-b3.html:
Let A=(1111),B=(1−1−11).

  1. Compute the eigenvalues of A, of B and of A+B.
  2. Verify @cor-ky-fan-subadditive for k=1 and k=2, and say for which k it is strict.
  3. Give a pair of Hermitian 2×2 matrices for which the k=1 inequality is an equality.

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c1.title: C1: The Loewner order and the partial sums
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c1.title_html: C1: The Loewner order and the partial sums
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. Prove that A⪰B implies ∑i≤kλi(A)≥∑i≤kλi(B) for every k. Hint: compare the two maximization problems of @thm-ky-fan competitor by competitor.
  2. Show that the converse fails: give Hermitian A,B satisfying all n of these inequalities with A⪰̸B.

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c2.title: C2: Partial sums that behave like a norm
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c2.title_html: C2: Partial sums that behave like a norm
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c2.html:
For positive semidefinite A∈Mn(F) and 1≤k≤n, consider sk(A)=∑i≤kλi(A), the partial sum of this section, now restricted to the positive semidefinite matrices.

  1. Prove that Nk(A)≥0, with equality if and only if A=0.
  2. Prove that Nk(cA)=cNk(A) for every real c≥0, and that Nk(A+B)≤Nk(A)+Nk(B) for positive semidefinite A,B.
  3. The positive semidefinite matrices form a cone, not a vector space, so a norm cannot be defined on them. Deduce instead that sk is positive, positively homogeneous and subadditive on this cone. Which step of your argument for (a) uses positive semidefiniteness, and what goes wrong without it?

exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c3.title: C3: How much of a matrix a subspace holds
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c3.title_html: C3: How much of a matrix a subspace holds
exr-poincare-and-ky-fan-c3.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) with singular values σ1≥⋯≥σp extended by zeros as in @cor-capture-bound-revisited, let S⊆Fm have dimension k, and let Q have as columns an orthonormal basis of S, so that PS=QQ∗ by @thm-projection-formula (a).

  1. Prove that ‖PSA‖F2=tr(Q∗AA∗Q).
  2. Deduce from @thm-ky-fan that ‖PSA‖F2≤σ12+⋯+σk2, with equality when S is spanned by the first k left singular vectors.
  3. Hence recover the value ∑i>kσi2 of the minimum in @cor-best-fitting-subspace. Hint: a−PSa is orthogonal to PSa.

exr-rank-one-updates-a1.title: A1
exr-rank-one-updates-a1.html:
1. State @thm-rank-one-interlacing, including the hypothesis on τ.
  2. Write down the secular function of A+2vv⊤ for A=diag(6,2,−1) and v=(1,3,1).
  3. Explain in one sentence why no di is an eigenvalue of A+τvv∗ under the hypotheses of @thm-secular-equation.
  4. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if τ<0 then λi(A+τvv∗)≥λi(A) for every i.
  5. A Hermitian 4×4 matrix A has eigenvalues 8,5,5,0. What does @cor-eigenvalue-shift-total say about A+3vv∗ when ‖v‖=2?

exr-rank-one-updates-b1.title: B1: A secular equation, end to end
exr-rank-one-updates-b1.title_html: B1: A secular equation, end to end
exr-rank-one-updates-b1.html:
Let A=diag(7,0,−3), v=(3,2,2) and τ=1.

  1. Write down A~=A+vv⊤ and the secular function f.
  2. Verify that 21, 2 and −2 are roots of f, and explain why these are all the eigenvalues of A~.
  3. Exhibit the interlacing chain of @thm-rank-one-interlacing for this pair.

exr-rank-one-updates-b2.title: B2: Reading the chain backwards
exr-rank-one-updates-b2.html:
Let B=(5225) and v=(1,2).

  1. Compute the eigenvalues of B and of B−vv⊤.
  2. State which chain of inequalities @thm-rank-one-interlacing gives here, being careful about which matrix plays the role of A.

exr-rank-one-updates-b3.title: B3: The missing eigenvalue
exr-rank-one-updates-b3.html: Let A=diag(5,3,0), v=(2,2,2) and τ=1. It is given that two of the eigenvalues of A~=A+vv⊤ are 15 and 4. Find the third without computing a characteristic polynomial, and then confirm it from the secular equation.

exr-rank-one-updates-c1.title: C1: What a zero coordinate does
exr-rank-one-updates-c1.title_html: C1: What a zero coordinate does
exr-rank-one-updates-c1.html:
Let A=diag(d1,…,dn) with the di real, let τ∈R and let v∈Fn.

  1. Prove that if vi=0 then ei is an eigenvector of A+τvv∗ with eigenvalue di.
  2. Suppose τ>0, the di are strictly decreasing, and exactly one coordinate vk vanishes. Show that the remaining n−1 eigenvalues of A+τvv∗ are the roots of the function obtained from the secular function by deleting the k-th term. Hint: restrict to the coordinate subspace spanned by the ei with i≠k.
  3. Illustrate both parts with A=diag(2,1,0), v=(1,0,1) and τ=1.

exr-rank-one-updates-c2.title: C2: Only one eigenvalue can escape
exr-rank-one-updates-c2.title_html: C2: Only one eigenvalue can escape
exr-rank-one-updates-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, v∈Fn, τ∈R, and A~=A+τvv∗.

  1. Prove that at most one eigenvalue of A~ lies outside the closed interval [λn(A),λ1(A)], and say which one it is and on which side, according to the sign of τ.
  2. Prove that the escaping eigenvalue moves by at most |τ|‖v‖2, and show by examples with n=2 that it may move by exactly that amount, and that it may not escape at all.

exr-rank-one-updates-c3.title: C3: Bumping along an eigenvector
exr-rank-one-updates-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u1,…,un, where Aui=λi(A)ui.

  1. Fix k and τ∈R. Prove that the eigenvalues of A+τukuk∗, listed with multiplicity but not necessarily in order, are λk(A)+τ together with λi(A) for i≠k.
  2. Deduce that A−λ1(A)u1u1∗ has eigenvalue list 0,λ2(A),…,λn(A). (This is the deflation step: it removes the top eigenvalue and leaves the rest untouched, which is what makes it possible to find eigenvalues one at a time.)
  3. Explain why (a) does not contradict part (c) of @thm-secular-equation.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-a1.title: A1
exr-rayleigh-quotient-a1.html:
1. State @def-rayleigh-quotient, naming both hypotheses, and say what each one is for.
  2. Prove that RA(cx)=RA(x) for every scalar c≠0, and explain why this makes RA a function on lines.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if A∈M3(R) is symmetric with three distinct eigenvalues, then RA takes exactly three values.
  4. State @prp-rayleigh-deflation, and say in one sentence why it is not a satisfactory description of λk(A).
  5. Give a Hermitian A and a vector x that is not an eigenvector of A but has RA(x) equal to an eigenvalue of A.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-b1.title: B1: Locating four values
exr-rayleigh-quotient-b1.html: Let A=(220232024)∈M3(R). Its eigenvalues are 6,3,0, with eigenvectors (1,2,2), (2,1,−2) and (2,−2,1) respectively; you may take this as given. Compute RA(x) for x=e1, x=(1,1,1), x=(1,1,0) and x=(1,0,−1), and check each value against @prp-rayleigh-basic. Hence exhibit a non-eigenvector at which RA equals an eigenvalue.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-b2.title: B2: A prescribed value
exr-rayleigh-quotient-b2.html: With A and the orthonormal eigenbasis of @exr-rayleigh-quotient-b1, use the construction in the proof of @prp-rayleigh-basic to produce a unit vector x with RA(x)=2. Then find, by mixing q1 and q2 in equal proportion, a vector with integer entries whose Rayleigh quotient is 9/2.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-b3.title: B3: The quotient of a projection
exr-rayleigh-quotient-b3.title_html: B3: The quotient of a projection
exr-rayleigh-quotient-b3.html:
Let U=span{(1,1,0),(0,0,1)}⊆R3 and let P be the matrix of the orthogonal projection onto U.

  1. Compute P, and list the eigenvalues of P with multiplicity.
  2. Compute RP(x) for x=e1, x=(1,−1,0) and x=(1,−1,1), and check each against @prp-rayleigh-basic.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-c1.title: C1: Why the quotient estimates eigenvalues so well
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c1.title_html: C1: Why the quotient estimates eigenvalues so well
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with orthonormal eigenbasis (q1,…,qn), Aqi=λi(A)qi.

  1. Prove that for every unit vector x, λ1(A)−RA(x) ≤ (λ1(A)−λn(A))‖x−q1‖2.
  2. Deduce that if ‖x−q1‖≤ε then RA(x) approximates λ1(A) with error at most (λ1−λn)ε2: an error in the eigenvector of size ε costs only ε2 in the eigenvalue.
  3. Show that the exponent 2 cannot be improved, by computing both sides for A=diag(1,0) and x=(cos⁡ε,sin⁡ε).

Hint for (a): expand x in the eigenbasis and compare the two sums term by term.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-c2.title: C2: The equality case at the top
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c2.title_html: C2: The equality case at the top
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let Eλ1(A)=ker(A−λ1(A)I) be the eigenspace of the largest eigenvalue.

  1. Prove that if x≠0 and RA(x)=λ1(A), then x∈Eλ1(A).
  2. Deduce that {x≠0:RA(x)=λ1(A)}∪{0}=Eλ1(A).
  3. Show that the corresponding statement for an intermediate eigenvalue is false, by naming a matrix, an index k with 1<k<n, and a vector.

exr-rayleigh-quotient-c3.title: C3: What the quotient cannot see
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c3.title_html: C3: What the quotient cannot see
exr-rayleigh-quotient-c3.html:
Let M∈Mn(F) be an arbitrary matrix, not assumed Hermitian, and put A=12(M+M∗),B=12(M−M∗), so that M=A+B with A∗=A and B∗=−B.

  1. Prove that Re⟨Mx,x⟩=⟨Ax,x⟩ for every x∈Fn.
  2. Deduce that over R, the function x↦⟨Mx,x⟩ determines A and nothing whatever about B. Give two distinct real 2×2 matrices with the same such function.
  3. Over C, determine whether ⟨Mx,x⟩=0 for all x forces M=0. Justify your answer.

exr-singular-values-variationally-a1.title: A1
exr-singular-values-variationally-a1.html:
1. State the min–max description of σk(A), naming the dimension of the subspaces in each of the two forms.
  2. Explain in one sentence why the identity ‖Ax‖2/‖x‖2=RA∗A(x) is what makes the whole section possible.
  3. State the bound of @cor-singular-value-perturbation and say precisely which hypotheses it needs, comparing with @cor-weyl-perturbation.
  4. What is min{‖A−B‖2:rankB≤k}, and what is the corresponding Frobenius-norm minimum? Which of the two is larger, and why?
  5. Decide whether the statement is correct, and justify: “a square matrix with a very small determinant is close to a singular matrix”.

exr-singular-values-variationally-b1.title: B1: Two norms, one list of singular values
exr-singular-values-variationally-b1.title_html: B1: Two norms, one list of singular values
exr-singular-values-variationally-b1.html:
A matrix A∈M5×4(R) has singular values 8,4,4,1.

  1. Compute min{‖A−B‖2:rankB≤k} for k=0,1,2,3.
  2. Compute the corresponding Frobenius minima and say for which k the two agree.
  3. Compute κ2(A) and the relative distance from A to the set of matrices of rank at most 3.

exr-singular-values-variationally-b2.title: B2: The nearest singular matrix
exr-singular-values-variationally-b2.html:
Let A=(2111), whose condition number κ2(A)=7+352≈6.854 was computed in @exm-condition-numbers-2x2.

  1. Find the singular values of A and the distance from A to the nearest singular matrix.
  2. Write down a singular matrix at exactly that distance, and check that it is singular.
  3. Compute the relative distance and compare it with 1/κ2(A).

exr-singular-values-variationally-b3.title: B3: Interlacing by hand
exr-singular-values-variationally-b3.html:
Let A=(200102).

  1. Compute the singular values of A.
  2. Compute the singular values of each of the three matrices obtained by deleting one row, and check @thm-singular-value-interlacing in each case.

exr-singular-values-variationally-c1.title: C1: Rank cannot drop suddenly
exr-singular-values-variationally-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank r≥1.

  1. Prove that every B∈Mm×n(F) with ‖A−B‖2<σr(A) has rankB≥r.
  2. Deduce that for every A there is an ε>0 such that every B within ε of A in the spectral norm has rankB≥rankA.
  3. Show that the reverse inequality can fail however small ε is: give matrices A and B with ‖A−B‖2 as small as we like and rankB>rankA.

Hint: for (a), argue by contradiction with @thm-eckart-young-spectral.

exr-singular-values-variationally-c2.title: C2: The dilation, and a second proof of the perturbation bound
exr-singular-values-variationally-c2.title_html: C2: The dilation, and a second proof of the perturbation bound
exr-singular-values-variationally-c2.html:
Let A,E∈Mm×n(F) and let H(⋅) be the Hermitian dilation of @prp-hermitian-dilation.

  1. Prove that H(A+E)=H(A)+H(E) and that H(E) is Hermitian.
  2. Prove that ‖H(E)‖2=‖E‖2.
  3. Hence give a second proof of @cor-singular-value-perturbation for 1≤i≤p, using @cor-weyl-perturbation, and say in one sentence why this route explains the absence of hypotheses on E.

Hint: for (b), use @prp-hermitian-dilation and @thm-operator-norm-formulas (c).

exr-weyl-inequalities-a1.title: A1
exr-weyl-inequalities-a1.html:
1. State both families of @thm-weyl-inequalities, with their index conditions, and say why the condition i+j−1≤n cannot be dropped from the first.
  2. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: for Hermitian A,B, λ2(A+B)≤λ2(A)+λ2(B).
  3. @cor-eigenvalues-continuous already said that eigenvalues move continuously. What does @cor-weyl-perturbation add?
  4. Explain why @cor-weyl-perturbation cannot be applied to A=J2(0) and E=εE21, and what goes wrong if one applies it anyway.
  5. If B is Hermitian of rank 3 and A is Hermitian of size 10, which eigenvalue of A+B is guaranteed to be at most λ4(A)?

exr-weyl-inequalities-b1.title: B1: A small table
exr-weyl-inequalities-b1.html: Let A=(0440) and B=(300−3). Compute the eigenvalues of A, B and A+B, write out every inequality of @thm-weyl-inequalities for this pair, and verify @cor-weyl-perturbation with E=B.

exr-weyl-inequalities-b2.title: B2: An interval for each eigenvalue
exr-weyl-inequalities-b2.title_html: B2: An interval for each eigenvalue
exr-weyl-inequalities-b2.html:
Let A=(210121012), whose eigenvalues are 2±2 and 2, and let E=1100J, where J∈M3(R) is the all-ones matrix.

  1. Compute ‖E‖2 and give an interval containing each eigenvalue of A+E.
  2. Deduce that A+E is positive definite.

exr-weyl-inequalities-b3.title: B3: What a low-rank update can do
exr-weyl-inequalities-b3.title_html: B3: What a low-rank update can do
exr-weyl-inequalities-b3.html: Let A∈M5(C) be Hermitian with λ(A)=(5,4,3,2,1), and let B∈M5(C) be Hermitian with rankB≤2. Find the best bounds that @cor-weyl-rank-bound gives for λ3(A+B), and give examples showing that each is attained.

exr-weyl-inequalities-c1.title: C1: The Loewner order through Weyl
exr-weyl-inequalities-c1.title_html: C1: The Loewner order through Weyl
exr-weyl-inequalities-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. Prove that if A⪰B then λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i, as a consequence of @cor-weyl-monotone.
  2. Hence deduce that |λi(A)−λi(B)|≤‖A−B‖2 for every i, without invoking @cor-weyl-perturbation.

exr-weyl-inequalities-c2.title: C2: The largest eigenvalue is a convex function
exr-weyl-inequalities-c2.title_html: C2: The largest eigenvalue is a convex function
exr-weyl-inequalities-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let t∈[0,1].

  1. Prove that λ1(tA+(1−t)B)≤tλ1(A)+(1−t)λ1(B).
  2. Deduce that for every c∈R the set {M∈Mn(F):M∗=M, λ1(M)≤c} is convex.
  3. Show that λ2 is not convex in this sense, by producing two Hermitian 2×2 matrices and a value of t where the inequality fails.

exr-weyl-inequalities-c3.title: C3: Sharpness of the whole family
exr-weyl-inequalities-c3.title_html: C3: Sharpness of the whole family
exr-weyl-inequalities-c3.html:
Fix n and indices i,j with i+j−1≤n. Construct Hermitian A,B∈Mn(R), both diagonal, for which λi+j−1(A+B)=λi(A)+λj(B).

Hint: with diagonal matrices every quantity in sight is a sorting problem; arrange for the (i+j−1)-st largest entry of the sum to sit in a coordinate where A contributes its i-th largest and B its j-th largest.

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-a1.title: A1
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-a1.html:
1. Define a flag of type (i1,…,ik) in Fn and a list adapted to it.
  2. State the max–min formula of @thm-wielandt-minimax, and name the index sets for which it reduces to @thm-courant-fischer and to @thm-ky-fan.
  3. Determine whether the following is true, and justify your answer: if (x1,…,xk) is adapted to a flag (W1,…,Wk), then span(x1,…,xj)=Wj for every j.
  4. Determine whether the following is true for all Hermitian A,B∈Mn(F), and justify your answer: λ2(A)−λ2(B)≤λ2(A−B).
  5. In the proof of @thm-lidskii-inequality, which part of @thm-wielandt-minimax is applied to A, which to B, and with which flag?

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b1.title: B1: Running the selection
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b1.html:
Let A=diag(4,1,−1)∈M3(R), take the index set (1,3), and let W be the flag W1=span((1,1,1))⊂W2=R3.

  1. Compute λ1(A)+λ3(A), and show directly that every list adapted to the eigenflag span(e1)⊂R3 has sum at least this number.
  2. Follow the proof of @thm-wielandt-minimax (a) for W: find J(W1) and J(W2), select x1,x2, apply Gram–Schmidt, and compute ∑j⟨Ayj,yj⟩.
  3. Compute the compression B of A to span(y1,y2) and its eigenvalues, and check λj(B)≤λij(A) for j=1,2.
  4. Find the minimum of ∑j⟨Axj,xj⟩ over all lists adapted to W. Is it the value found in (b)?

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b2.title: B2: A complex pair
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b2.html:
Let A=(21+i1−i1),B=(100−1)in M2(C).

  1. Check that A and B are Hermitian, and compute 𝛌λ(A), 𝛌λ(B) and 𝛌λ(A−B).
  2. Verify @thm-lidskii-inequality for all three index sets, and say which inequality is an equality and why it had to be.
  3. Verify both bounds of @cor-lidskii-special-cases (a), and explain why here every λi(A)−λi(B) had to be non-negative.

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b3.title: B3: The lower bound
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-b3.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n. Prove that ∑j=1kλij(A)−∑j=1kλij(B) ≥ ∑j=n−k+1nλj(A−B), that is, the shifts over any k indices add up to at least the k smallest eigenvalues of A−B. Check the result on @exm-lidskii-3x3.

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-c1.title: C1: A second proof of Lidskii’s inequality
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-c1.title_html: C1: A second proof of Lidskii’s inequality
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-c1.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, put C=A−B, and fix an index set 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n.

  1. Let c∈R. Show that replacing A by A−cI, with B unchanged, lowers both sides of @thm-lidskii-inequality by kc. Deduce that it suffices to prove the inequality when λk(C)=0.
  2. Assume λk(C)=0. Write C=UDU∗ with U unitary and D=diag(λ1(C),…,λn(C)), and put C+=UD+U∗, where D+ replaces each negative diagonal entry of D by 0. Prove that C+⪰C, C+⪰0 and trC+=∑j≤kλj(C).
  3. Prove that λi(A)≤λi(B+C+) and λi(B+C+)≥λi(B) for every i, and deduce @thm-lidskii-inequality.
  4. Which of the ingredients of this proof were available before this section? What does this proof not give that @thm-wielandt-minimax does?

Hint: @cor-loewner-eigenvalue-monotone.

exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-c2.title: C2: The total absolute shift
exr-wielandt-and-lidskii-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian.

  1. Prove that ∑i=1n|λi(A)−λi(B)| ≤ ∑i=1n|λi(A−B)|.
  2. Show that equality holds when A⪰B. Compute both sides for @exm-lidskii-3x3, and compare with the bound n‖A−B‖2 obtained by adding the bounds of @cor-weyl-perturbation.

Hint for (a): use the set of indices at which λi(A)>λi(B).

lem-am-gm.title: The Arithmetic–Geometric Mean Inequality
lem-am-gm.html: Let n≥1 and let t1,…,tn be non-negative real numbers. Then t1t2⋯tn≤(t1+t2+⋯+tnn)n, with equality if and only if t1=t2=⋯=tn.

lem-coordinate-compression.title: Deleting a Row and a Column Is Restricting to a Hyperplane
lem-coordinate-compression.title_html: Deleting a Row and a Column Is Restricting to a Hyperplane
lem-coordinate-compression.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with n≥2, fix m with 1≤m≤n, put I={1,…,n}∖{m} and B=AI,I∈Mn−1(F). Let H={x∈Fn:xm=0}, and let φ:H→Fn−1 delete the m-th coordinate. Then φ is a linear isomorphism, and for every x∈H, ⟨Ax,x⟩=⟨Bφ(x),φ(x)⟩,‖x‖=‖φ(x)‖. In particular RA(x)=RB(φ(x)) for every x∈H with x≠0.

lem-eigenvalues-of-a-function.title: The Eigenvalue List of an Increasing Function
lem-eigenvalues-of-a-function.title_html: The Eigenvalue List of an Increasing Function
lem-eigenvalues-of-a-function.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with spec(A)⊆I, and let f:I→R be increasing. Then f(A) is Hermitian and λi(f(A))=f(λi(A))(i=1,…,n).

lem-eigenvalues-of-negation.title: Negation Reverses the List
lem-eigenvalues-of-negation.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then −A is Hermitian and λp(−A)=−λn+1−p(A)(1≤p≤n).

lem-hermitian-spectral-norm.title: The Spectral Norm of a Hermitian Matrix
lem-hermitian-spectral-norm.title_html: The Spectral Norm of a Hermitian Matrix
lem-hermitian-spectral-norm.html: Let E∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then ‖E‖2=max1≤i≤n|λi(E)|=max(λ1(E), −λn(E)).

lem-horn-two-by-two.title: The Two-by-Two Rotation
lem-horn-two-by-two.html: Let λ1≥λ2 and t be real numbers with λ2≤t≤λ1. Put b=(λ1−t)(t−λ2). Then there is an orthogonal R∈O(2) with Rdiag(λ1,λ2)R⊤=(tbbλ1+λ2−t).

lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan.title: The Quotient on a Span of Eigenvectors
lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan.title_html: The Quotient on a Span of Eigenvectors
lem-rayleigh-on-eigenspan.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let (u1,…,un) be an orthonormal basis of Fn with Aup=λp(A)up for every p. Fix i with 1≤i≤n.

  1. If x≠0 lies in span{ui,ui+1,…,un}, then RA(x)≤λi(A).
  2. If x≠0 lies in span{u1,u2,…,ui}, then RA(x)≥λi(A).

lem-rayleigh-range-on-subspace.title: The Rayleigh Quotient on a Subspace
lem-rayleigh-range-on-subspace.title_html: The Rayleigh Quotient on a Subspace
lem-rayleigh-range-on-subspace.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let W⊆Fn be a subspace with dim⁡W=m≥1. Let Q∈Mn×m(F) be a matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of W, and put B=Q∗AQ∈Mm(F). Then B is Hermitian and {RA(x):0≠x∈W}=[λm(B), λ1(B)]. In particular max0≠x∈WRA(x) and min0≠x∈WRA(x) exist and are attained.

lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates.title: Stretching in the Right Singular Basis
lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates.title_html: Stretching in the Right Singular Basis
lem-stretch-in-singular-coordinates.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have a singular value decomposition A=UΣV∗ (@thm-svd), with v1,…,vn the columns of V, and write σi=σi(A) with the convention above. Then for x=∑i=1ncivi, ‖Ax‖2=∑i=1nσi2|ci|2,‖x‖2=∑i=1n|ci|2. Consequently, for each 1≤k≤n:

  1. on the tail subspace Tk=span(vk,…,vn), of dimension n−k+1, max{‖Ax‖‖x‖:0≠x∈Tk}=σk, attained at x=vk;
  2. on the head subspace Hk=span(v1,…,vk), of dimension k, min{‖Ax‖‖x‖:0≠x∈Hk}=σk, attained at x=vk.

lem-subspace-intersection.title: Large Subspaces Intersect
lem-subspace-intersection.html: Let V be a vector space with dim⁡V=n over any field, and let U and W be subspaces of V with dim⁡U+dim⁡W>n. Then U∩W≠{0}. More precisely, dim⁡(U∩W)≥dim⁡U+dim⁡W−n.

lem-tridiagonal-eigenvector-ends.title: Eigenvectors of an Unreduced Tridiagonal Matrix
lem-tridiagonal-eigenvector-ends.title_html: Eigenvectors of an Unreduced Tridiagonal Matrix
lem-tridiagonal-eigenvector-ends.html: Let T∈Mk(R) be symmetric and tridiagonal, with every entry ti,i+1=ti+1,i (1≤i≤k−1) non-zero. Then every eigenvector u of T has uk≠0. Consequently every eigenspace of T has dimension 1, so T has k distinct eigenvalues.

prp-affine-operator-monotone.title: Increasing Affine Functions
prp-affine-operator-monotone.html: Let α,β∈R with β≥0. Then f(t)=α+βt is operator monotone on R. Moreover, every affine function t↦α+βt, with β of either sign, is both operator convex and operator concave on R.

prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing.title: Every Increasing Function Is Monotone on Eigenvalues
prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing.title_html: Every Increasing Function Is Monotone on Eigenvalues
prp-eigenvalue-monotone-increasing.html: Let f:I→R be increasing, and let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with spectra in I and A⪰B. Then λi(f(A)) ≥ λi(f(B))for every i=1,…,n.

prp-hermitian-dilation.title: The Hermitian Dilation
prp-hermitian-dilation.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and put H(A):=(0AA∗0)∈Mm+n(F). Then H(A) is Hermitian, and its eigenvalues, with multiplicity, are σ1(A),…,σp(A), −σ1(A),…,−σp(A), 0,…,0⏟m+n−2p.

prp-inverse-operator-monotone.title: The Negative Reciprocal Is Operator Monotone
prp-inverse-operator-monotone.title_html: The Negative Reciprocal Is Operator Monotone
prp-inverse-operator-monotone.html: The function t↦−1/t is operator monotone on (0,∞). Explicitly: if A,B∈Mn(F) are Hermitian with A⪰B≻0, then A≻0 and −A−1 ⪰ −B−1,that is,B−1⪰A−1.

prp-majorization-basic.title: Basic Properties of Majorization
prp-majorization-basic.html:
Let x,y,z∈Rn.

  1. x≺x.
  2. If x≺y and y≺z, then x≺z.
  3. If x≺y and y≺x, then x↓=y↓; that is, y is a rearrangement of x.

Statements (a) and (b) hold with ≺w in place of ≺.

prp-operator-monotone-cone.title: Combining Operator Monotone Functions
prp-operator-monotone-cone.html:
Let f and g be operator monotone on I.

  1. For every c≥0 and every α∈R, the functions f+g and α+cf are operator monotone on I.
  2. For every s∈R, the translate t↦f(t+s) is operator monotone on the interval I−s={t−s:t∈I}.

prp-operator-monotone-increasing.title: Operator Monotone Functions Are Increasing
prp-operator-monotone-increasing.html: If f is operator monotone on I, then f is increasing on I.

prp-rayleigh-basic.title: The Range of the Rayleigh Quotient
prp-rayleigh-basic.title_html: The Range of the Rayleigh Quotient
prp-rayleigh-basic.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, n≥1. Then {RA(x):x∈Fn, x≠0}=[λn(A), λ1(A)], the whole closed interval. In particular λ1(A)=maxx≠0RA(x),λn(A)=minx≠0RA(x), and both are attained, at unit eigenvectors for λ1(A) and λn(A).

prp-rayleigh-critical-points.title: Critical Points of the Rayleigh Quotient
prp-rayleigh-critical-points.title_html: Critical Points of the Rayleigh Quotient
prp-rayleigh-critical-points.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let x∈Fn be a unit vector and put μ=RA(x)=⟨Ax,x⟩. For every v∈Fn and every t∈R with x+tv≠0, RA(x+tv)−μ=2tRe⟨Ax−μx,v⟩+t2(⟨Av,v⟩−μ‖v‖2)‖x+tv‖2.{#eq-rayleigh-expansion} Moreover:

  1. Re⟨Ax−μx,v⟩=0 for every v∈Fn if and only if Ax=μx; that is, if and only if x is an eigenvector of A, necessarily for the eigenvalue μ.
  2. If RA(x)≥RA(y) for every y≠0, then the condition in (a) holds. The same is true if RA(x)≤RA(y) for every y≠0.

prp-rayleigh-deflation.title: Eigenvalues by Deflation
prp-rayleigh-deflation.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let (q1,…,qn) be an orthonormal basis of Fn with Aqi=λi(A)qi for every i. Then for every k with 1≤k≤n, λk(A)=max{RA(x):x≠0, x⊥q1,…,qk−1}, the maximum being attained at x=qk. For k=1 the list of constraints is empty and the statement is @prp-rayleigh-basic.

prp-square-operator-convex.title: The Square Is Operator Convex
prp-square-operator-convex.html: The function t↦t2 is operator convex on R. Explicitly: for Hermitian A,B∈Mn(F) and θ∈[0,1], θA2+(1−θ)B2−(θA+(1−θ)B)2=θ(1−θ)(A−B)2 ⪰ 0.

thm-bordered-matrix.title: Bordering a Hermitian Matrix
thm-bordered-matrix.html:
Let B∈Mn−1(F) be Hermitian with n≥2, let b∈Fn−1, let c∈R, and let A=(Bbb∗c)∈Mn(F), which is Hermitian and has AI,I=B for I={1,…,n−1}. For an eigenvalue ν of B, write Pν for the orthogonal projection of Fn−1 onto the eigenspace Eν(B), and mν=dim⁡Eν(B).

  1. If Pνb≠0, then ν is a root of pA of multiplicity exactly mν−1; in particular, if mν=1 then ν is not an eigenvalue of A.
  2. If Pνb=0, then ν is a root of pA of multiplicity at least mν.
  3. The interlacing λ1(A)≥λ1(B)≥⋯≥λn−1(B)≥λn(A) is strict at every one of its 2(n−1) inequalities if and only if B has n−1 distinct eigenvalues and Pνb≠0 for every eigenvalue ν of B.

thm-cauchy-interlacing.title: Cauchy’s Interlacing Theorem
thm-cauchy-interlacing.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with n≥2, let I⊆{1,…,n} with |I|=n−1, and let B=AI,I. Then λk(A) ≥ λk(B) ≥ λk+1(A)(1≤k≤n−1), that is, λ1(A)≥λ1(B)≥λ2(A)≥λ2(B)≥⋯≥λn−1(B)≥λn(A).

thm-courant-fischer.title: Courant–Fischer Min–Max Theorem
thm-courant-fischer.html: Let F be R or C, let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let 1≤k≤n. Then λk(A)=mindim⁡W=n−k+1  max0≠x∈W RA(x)=maxdim⁡W=k  min0≠x∈W RA(x), where in each line W runs over all subspaces of Fn of the stated dimension. All four extrema are attained.

thm-eckart-young-spectral.title: Eckart–Young Theorem, Spectral Case
thm-eckart-young-spectral.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and let 0≤k<n. Then for every B∈Mm×n(F) with rankB≤k, ‖A−B‖2 ≥ σk+1(A), and equality holds for the truncation B=Ak of @def-truncated-svd. In words: Ak minimizes ‖A−B‖2 over all matrices of rank at most k, and the minimum value is σk+1(A).

thm-haynsworth.title: Haynsworth’s Inertia Additivity Formula
thm-haynsworth.html: Let 1≤k≤n−1 and let M=(ABB∗D)∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, with A∈Mk(F) invertible, B∈Mk×(n−k)(F) and D∈Mn−k(F). Then A and the Schur complement M/A=D−B∗A−1B (@def-schur-complement) are Hermitian, and In(M)=In(A)+In(M/A).

thm-horn.title: Horn’s Theorem
thm-horn.html: Let n≥1, and let d=(d1,…,dn) and 𝛌λ=(λ1,…,λn) be vectors in Rn with 𝛌d≺λ. Then there is an orthogonal Q∈O(n) such that the matrix A=Qdiag(λ1,…,λn)Q⊤ has diagonal entries d1,d2,…,dn, in this order. So A is a real symmetric matrix with d(A)=d and 𝛌𝛌λ(A)=λ↓.

thm-inertia-rank-perturbation.title: Inertia Moves by at Most the Rank
thm-inertia-rank-perturbation.title_html: Inertia Moves by at Most the Rank
thm-inertia-rank-perturbation.html: Let A,E∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with rankE≤r. Then |n+(A+E)−n+(A)|≤r,|n−(A+E)−n−(A)|≤r, and |n0(A+E)−n0(A)|≤r as well.

thm-inertia-second-proof.title: Sylvester’s Law of Inertia, Second Proof
thm-inertia-second-proof.title_html: Sylvester’s Law of Inertia, Second Proof
thm-inertia-second-proof.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Call a subspace W≤Fn A-positive if ⟨Ax,x⟩>0 for every x∈W with x≠0. Then:

  1. n+(A)=max{dim⁡W:W is A-positive}, and the maximum is attained at the span of an orthonormal family of eigenvectors for the positive eigenvalues of A;
  2. for every invertible P∈Mn(F), the matrix P∗AP is Hermitian and In(P∗AP)=In(A).

Over R, part (b) is Sylvester’s Law of Inertia, @thm-sylvester-inertia.

thm-ky-fan.title: Ky Fan Maximum Principle
thm-ky-fan.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let 1≤k≤n. Then ∑i=1kλi(A)=max{∑i=1k⟨Aqi,qi⟩ : q1,…,qk orthonormal}=max{tr(Q∗AQ) : Q∈Mn×k(F), Q∗Q=Ik}, and the maximum is attained by Q=(u1 … uk) for any orthonormal basis (u1,…,un) of Fn with Aui=λi(A)ui.

thm-lidskii-inequality.title: Lidskii’s Inequality
thm-lidskii-inequality.html: Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, with F=R or C. Then for every index set 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n, ∑j=1kλij(A)−∑j=1kλij(B) ≤ ∑j=1kλj(A−B).

thm-loewner-statement.title: Loewner’s Theorem, Statement
thm-loewner-statement.html:
Let f:(0,∞)→R. The following are equivalent.

  1. f is operator monotone on (0,∞).
  2. There are α∈R, β≥0 and a positive measure ν on [0,∞) with ∫[0,∞)dν(s)1+s2<∞, such that for every t>0 f(t)=α+βt+∫[0,∞)(s1+s2−1t+s)dν(s).
  3. f is the restriction to (0,∞) of a function that is analytic on C∖(−∞,0] and sends every point of the upper half-plane {z:Imz>0} to a point with non-negative imaginary part.

thm-poincare-separation.title: Poincaré Separation Theorem
thm-poincare-separation.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let 1≤k≤n, and let B=Q∗AQ be the compression of A to a k-dimensional subspace W⊆Fn, as in @def-compression. Then λi(A) ≥ λi(B) ≥ λi+n−k(A)(1≤i≤k).

thm-rank-one-interlacing.title: Interlacing for a Rank-One Update
thm-rank-one-interlacing.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, let v∈Fn, let τ≥0, and put A~=A+τvv∗. Then λi(A~) ≥ λi(A) ≥ λi+1(A~)(1≤i≤n−1), and λn(A~)≥λn(A). Written as one chain, λ1(A~) ≥ λ1(A) ≥ λ2(A~) ≥ λ2(A) ≥ … ≥ λn(A~) ≥ λn(A).

thm-schur-horn.title: Schur–Horn Theorem
thm-schur-horn.html: Let F=R or F=C, and let 𝛌d,λ∈Rn. There is a Hermitian A∈Mn(F) with 𝛌𝛌λ(A)=λ↓ and d(A)=d if and only if 𝛌d≺λ. In words: the diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with spectrum 𝛌λ are exactly the vectors majorized by 𝛌λ, and real symmetric matrices already give all of them.

thm-schur-majorization.title: Schur’s Majorization Theorem
thm-schur-majorization.html: Let F=R or F=C, and let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. Then 𝛌d(A)≺λ(A). Explicitly, if d(A)↓=(a1↓,…,an↓) lists the diagonal entries of A decreasingly, then a1↓+⋯+ak↓≤λ1(A)+⋯+λk(A)(1≤k≤n−1),a1↓+⋯+an↓=λ1(A)+⋯+λn(A).

thm-secular-equation.title: Eigenvalues from the Secular Equation
thm-secular-equation.html:
Let A=diag(d1,…,dn) with d1>d2>⋯>dn strictly decreasing and real, let τ>0, and let v∈Fn have every coordinate non-zero. Write A~=A+τvv∗ and let f be its secular function. Then:

  1. no di is an eigenvalue of A~;
  2. a real number λ∉{d1,…,dn} is an eigenvalue of A~ if and only if f(λ)=0;
  3. f has exactly n roots μ1>⋯>μn, one in each of the intervals (d1,∞), (d2,d1), …, (dn,dn−1), and none below dn; these are the eigenvalues of A~, each simple, and μ1>d1>μ2>d2>⋯>μn>dn;
  4. for each j, the vector (A−μjI)−1v is an eigenvector of A~ for μj.

thm-singular-value-interlacing.title: Interlacing Under Deletion of a Row or a Column
thm-singular-value-interlacing.title_html: Interlacing Under Deletion of a Row or a Column
thm-singular-value-interlacing.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) with m≥2, and let B∈M(m−1)×n(F) be obtained from A by deleting one row. Then σi(B)≤σi(A)(1≤i≤n),σi+1(A)≤σi(B)(1≤i≤n−1), singular values beyond the p-th being read as 0. If instead n≥2 and B∈Mm×(n−1)(F) is obtained from A by deleting one column, the same two chains hold, both over 1≤i≤n−1; written out, σ1(A)≥σ1(B)≥σ2(A)≥⋯≥σn−1(B)≥σn(A).

thm-singular-value-minmax.title: Min–Max for Singular Values
thm-singular-value-minmax.html: Let A∈Mm×n(F) and let 1≤k≤n, with σk(A)=0 read by convention when k>p. Then σk(A)=minW≤Fndim⁡W=n−k+1 max0≠x∈W ‖Ax‖‖x‖=maxW≤Fndim⁡W=k min0≠x∈W ‖Ax‖‖x‖. The outer minimum is attained at W=span(vk,…,vn) and the outer maximum at W=span(v1,…,vk), for the right singular vectors of any singular value decomposition of A (@thm-svd).

thm-weyl-inequalities.title: Weyl’s Inequalities
thm-weyl-inequalities.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let 1≤i,j≤n.

  1. If i+j−1≤n, then λi+j−1(A+B) ≤ λi(A)+λj(B).
  2. If i+j−n≥1, then λi+j−n(A+B) ≥ λi(A)+λj(B).

thm-weyl-singular-values.title: Weyl’s Inequalities for Singular Values
thm-weyl-singular-values.html: Let A,B∈Mm×n(F) and let i,j≥1 with i+j−1≤n. Then σi+j−1(A+B)≤σi(A)+σj(B).

thm-wielandt-minimax.title: Wielandt’s Minimax Principle
thm-wielandt-minimax.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, with F=R or C, and let 1≤i1<⋯<ik≤n.

  1. For every flag W of type (i1,…,ik) there is a list (x1,…,xk) adapted to W with ∑j=1k⟨Axj,xj⟩ ≤ ∑j=1kλij(A).
  2. Let (u1,…,un) be an orthonormal basis with Aup=λp(A)up for every p, and let WA be the flag Wj=span(u1,…,uij). Then every list (x1,…,xk) adapted to WA satisfies ∑j=1k⟨Axj,xj⟩ ≥ ∑j=1kλij(A), with equality for xj=uij.
  3. Consequently ∑j=1kλij(A)=maxW min(x1,…,xk) ∑j=1k⟨Axj,xj⟩, where W runs over all flags of type (i1,…,ik) in Fn, and for each W the list runs over all lists adapted to W. The inner minimum exists for every W, and the outer maximum is attained at WA.
